A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be [[Definition:Metacategory|categories]].
A [[Definition:Contravariant Functor|contravariant functor]] $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ satisfies:
:$\map F {g \circ f} = \map F f \circ \map F g$
:$\map F {\operatorname {id}_C} = \operatorname {id}_{\map F C}$
with $\map F f: \map F B \to \map F A$ for $f: A \to B$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be [[Definition:Metacategory|categories]].
A [[Definition:Covariant Functor|covariant functor]] $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ satisfies:
:$\map F {g \circ f} = \map F g \circ \map F f$
:$\map F {\operatorname {id}_C} = \operatorname {id}_{\map F C}$

object_map.reformulation: The contravariance must be absorbed into the source category rather than the functor, which is the reformulation that makes the two notions the same.

validity_conditions: the opposite category must be a genuine category, which holds since reversing all arrows preserves associativity and identities
objects are unchanged by the duality; only morphism direction reverses
the identification is a definition rather than a theorem, so nothing is proved by it beyond transporting results
proof_plan: Form the [[Definition:Dual Category|opposite category]] $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$ by keeping the objects of $\mathbf C$ and reversing every [[Definition:Morphism|morphism]], with $f \circ^{\text {op} } g = g \circ f$.
[[Definition:Associative Operation|Associativity]] and the identity laws in $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$ follow directly from those in $\mathbf C$.

A contravariant assignment $F$ on $\mathbf C$ is exactly a [[Definition:Covariant Functor|covariant functor]] $\mathbf C^{\text {op} } \to \mathbf D$:
:$\map F {f \circ^{\text {op} } g} = \map F {g \circ f} = \map F f \circ \map F g$
Hence any theorem about covariant functors yields its dual statement for contravariant functors by substituting $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$ for $\mathbf C$.
